name: Maka (Bebend)
overview: The Maka Bebend form a relatively isolated Maka clan but one linked to the other Maka groups of the East and to the Ngoumba of the South. Having come from Adamawa in the 17th century with the Maka Bwanz and Maka Ebe, they live from farming, hunting, fishing and crafts, and dance the mpiné around the fire, formerly on returning from war.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Isolated group where several clans live side by side; many also speak Yebekolo, the language of the neighbouring group.
Makaa is spoken in the East and, among the Ngoumba, in the South.
At first endogamous, the Bebend now marry their neighbours; it is mainly the girls who marry outside.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land, with no particular religious value.
Having left Adamawa in the 17th century with the Maka Bwanz and Maka Ebe, they split following a quarrel; all the Maka continue to collaborate.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Prestige lies in the number of wives and children and in power.
Decisions are taken in an assembly, by consensus among the elders.
Each generation lives among its own: children with children, adults with adults; the son-in-law avoids his in-laws.
Respect owed to parents by children, to elders by juniors.
Relations with neighbours mix alliances and memories of ancient wars.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Kinship both patrilineal and matrilineal; the young wife joins her husband in his village.
The boy becomes a man by building his house and marrying.
The reported ages at marriage are early.
Steps: presentation, marriage proposal, bride price, possibly marriage certificate.
Bride price: grinding mill (to feed the family), machete, hoe and file (work), demijohn of red wine (which honours the young woman).

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No common worship, but each clan has its own rites, celebrated at the end of the year; little is said about these cults, which are linked to forests and watercourses.
Birth welcomes a new person; death takes one back to the forebears.
Incest would bring elephantiasis; breaking food taboos, illness. Women do not eat snake.
Capital offences: incest and violence against one's parents.
Divination by animal skins and oracles in the forest.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, hunting, small-scale livestock rearing. Women: farming, fishing, crafts.
The land goes to the first occupant, according to the “right of the axe”.
Crafts: tam-tams, drums, baskets.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Clothing of bark, and of animal skins for the nobles.
Traditional medicine remains in use, out of habit and for its low cost.
Beauty: the strong, robust man, the full-figured woman with long hair.
Courtship: offering game, dancing well, singing, playing an instrument; kindness, generosity and good manners.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: alenga, akoulbang, mpiné, tsoune, on the tam-tam and drums.
Dances: tsoune at mourning, mpiné on return from war (around the fire), akoulbang in joy, alenga at festivals.
No community festival of its own.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: The group's history is marked by wars between peoples, the conquest of territory and relations with the colonial power, a history shared with the other Maka.

sections.title: The names
items: Twins: Mekoau for boys, Ngaali for girls.
The father chooses the name with his parents; it does not change.
Nickname: messob; moan marks descent.
The founding ancestor is called Bebend.

lessons.title: Who are the Maka (Bebend)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Maka (Bebend) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Maka (Bebend) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Maka (Bebend) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Maka (Bebend) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Maka (Bebend) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Maka (Bebend) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Isolated group in which several clans live side by side; many also speak Yebekolo, the language of the neighbouring group. • Makaa is spoken in the East and, among the Ngoumba, in the South. • First endogamous, the Bebend now marry their neighbours; it is mainly the girls who marry outside. • Ancestral land, with no particular religious value. • Having left Adamawa in the 17th century with the Maka Bwanz and Maka Ebe, they separated following a dispute; all the Maka continue to collaborate.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Maka Bebend form a relatively isolated Maka clan but one linked to the other Maka groups of the East and to the Ngoumba of the South. Having come from Adamawa in the 17th century with the Maka Bwanz and Maka Ebe, they live from farming, hunting, fishing and crafts, and dance the mpiné around the fire, formerly on returning from war.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Maka (Bebend) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Power and social organisation among the Maka (Bebend)
lessons.anelcac: Socio-political organisation, rules for living together
lessons.competence: Describe how the Maka (Bebend) organise power, make decisions and regulate community life.
lessons.situation: An important decision must be made for the whole Maka (Bebend) village. Who decides, and how?
lessons.materiel: The community's cultural profile, paper and felt-tip pens for the organisation chart.

steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “An important decision has to be made for the whole Maka (Bebend) village. Who decides, and how?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — Who holds authority? — How are decisions made (consensus, vote, the chief's decision)? — What rules of respect and deference are observed? — Which groups or societies play a particular role?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Prestige comes from the number of wives and children and from power. • Decisions are made in assembly, by consensus among the elders. • Each generation lives among its own: children with children, adults with adults; the son-in-law avoids his in-laws. • Respect is owed to parents by children, and to elders by juniors. • Relations with neighbours combine alliances and memories of ancient wars.

steps.instruction: Prestige lies in the number of wives and children and in power. Decisions are made in assembly, by consensus among the elders. Each generation lives among its own: children with children, adults with adults; the son-in-law avoids his in-laws.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a diagram (organisation chart) of power among the Maka (Bebend), then explain in 3 sentences how a decision is made.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Maka (Bebend)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Maka (Bebend), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Maka (Bebend).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Maka (Bebend), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Maka (Bebend).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: plantain purée (ndengue), pounded cassava leaves (kpwem), boiled cassava. • Drinks: palm wine, raffia wine, fermented banana. • Men: farming, hunting, small livestock rearing. Women: farming, fishing, crafts.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Maka (Bebend) mainly eat plantain purée, pounded cassava leaves, boiled cassava. Traditional drinks: palm wine, raffia wine, fermented banana. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Maka (Bebend): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.title: Birth, name and the passage to adulthood among the Maka (Bebend)
objectives: Explain the meaning of a birth
lessons.competence: Explain how the Maka (Bebend) welcome a child, give the child a name and mark the child's entry into adulthood.
lessons.situation: A child has just been born in a Maka (Bebend) family. How will he be named, and how will he become an adult?

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What does a birth mean for the community? — Who gives the name, when and how? — Can the name change during a lifetime? — When and how does one become a man or a woman?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Maka (Bebend), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Maka (Bebend). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • Men: farming, hunting, small-scale livestock rearing. Women: farming, fishing, crafts. • Land goes to the first occupant, according to the “axe right”. • Crafts: tom-toms, drums, baskets.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Men: farming, hunting, small-scale livestock rearing. Women: farming, fishing, crafts. Land goes to the first occupant, according to the “right of the axe”.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Maka (Bebend)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I classify

activities.title: I propose
activities.instruction: Suggest a project idea that promotes a local skill.

student.memo: Men: farming, hunting, small-scale livestock rearing. Women: farming, fishing, crafts. Land goes to the first occupant, according to the “right of the axe”.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Maka (Bebend)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: forêts et cours d'eau des clans

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Maka (Bebend), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Maka (Bebend). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Maka (Bebend), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Maka (Bebend). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • No common cult, but each clan has its own rites, celebrated at the end of the year; these cults, linked to forests and watercourses, are little spoken of. • Birth welcomes a new person; death returns one to the forebears. • Incest is said to bring elephantiasis; breaking food prohibitions, illness. Women do not eat snake. • Capital offences: incest and violence towards one's parents. • Divination with animal skins and oracles in the forest.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No common worship, but each clan has its own rites, celebrated at the end of the year; little is said about these cults, which are linked to forests and watercourses. Birth welcomes a new person; death brings one back to the ancestors.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Maka (Bebend) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Maka (Bebend) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: No common worship, but each clan has its own rites, celebrated at the end of the year; little is said about these cults, which are linked to forests and watercourses. Birth welcomes a new person; death brings one back to the ancestors.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Makaa
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Maka (Bebend) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Maka (Bebend) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Maka (Bebend) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Maka (Bebend) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Makaa. • Greeting formulae: Bihguelassq = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); Madjoum = morning greeting (one person); Bi madjoum = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Ngut, Iba, Iloual, Ino, Itone. • The founding ancestor is called Bebend. • The group's history is marked by wars between peoples, the conquest of territory and relations with the colonial power, a history shared with the other Maka.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Makaa are the first steps towards communicating with the Maka (Bebend). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Makaa.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Makaa are the first steps towards communicating with the Maka (Bebend). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
